caseno: FMAT No. 285 of 2001 With Civil Rule No. 255 (FM) of 2001.
lawyer:
Habibul Islam Bhuiyan with Gazi Neamat Hossain, Advocates------For the Appellant. 
Ajmalul Hossain, with Md Rafiqul Islam, Abdur Razzak, Arfan Ahmed Siddique, Mizanur Rahman, Iftekhar Ahmed and Md Aminul Islam Mandal, Advocates------For the Respondents.
parties:
Hamza Rubber Industries  ------ Appellant
Vs.
Golam Dastagir Gazi  ------ Respondents.
full_judgment:
This appeal was presented by the plaintiff against judgment and order dated 12-02-2001 passed by the 10th Court of Additional District Judge at Dhaka in Title Suit No. 32 of 2000 by which the prayer of the plaintiff for temporary injunction was refused. 

 2. The plaintiff instituted the suit for a decree for perpetual injunction for restraining the defendants from manufacturing and marketing rubber cycle/rickshaw tyres imitating Trade Mark of the plaintiff consisting of a device of double elephants or similar/confusingly device similar to that of the plaintiffs Trade Mark. The plaint Case, in short, is that on 27-01-1991 the plaintiff applied for registration of a device consisting of elephant as Trade Mark and on 18-05-1994 got registration. On 27-01-1998 on the prayer of the plaintiff, that registration was renewed for a further period of fifteen years. As the proprietor of the Trade Mark, the plaintiff has been n6ilufacturing and marketing cycle and rickshaw tyres and tubes using said device of elephant, and achieved popularity and goodwill and has thus become the leading tyre manufacturer and seller in the country. Tempted by the success of the plaintiff, the defendants adopted a device of two elephants embossed in cycle and rickshaw tyres in manner identical to that of the plaintiff. Use of two elephants by the defendants has caused confusion in the market and thereby, the defendants are passing off their tyres as those of the plaintiff. Customers and public in general are being deceived. The defendants have been manufacturing and selling rickshaw tyres using a device of two double elephants similar to the Trade Mark of the plaintiff. 

 3. After filing the plaint on the aforesaid averments the plaintiff made an application under Order XXXIX rules 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure for temporary injunction for restraining the defendants from producing and selling rickshaw tyres using the device of double elephants till disposal of the suit. 

 4. The defendants opposed the application by filing a written objection denying the case of the plaintiff. Their case, in brief, is that the industry established by the defendants in 1997 is of very good quality. Taka 12 crore was invested in the project and funds were raised from the creditors both national and international. About 350 employees are employed. They are manufacturing. and selling tyres using the device of double elephants facing each other with their trunks held high along with the embossment 'HAMZA TYRES' and HAMZA TUBES', and huge quantity of tyres are already marketed to the dealers all over the country. They have already applied for registration of their device of double elephants. Their device is so dissimilar to that of the plaintiff, single elephant and double elephants back to back one after another along with embossment 'GAZI TYRES' and GAZI TUBES' there is no scope for any confusion. On 19-02-2000 they obtained a search report from the office of the Registrar that none is using their trade mark. In order to secure their tyres, they also applied for copy right of their design. In the premises they contended that the plaintiff has no case for temporary injunction and the balance of convenience is in their favour. 

 6. Mr Habibul Islam Bhuiyan, learned Senior Counsel for the appellant submits that the trial Court though found that the plaintiff has got a prima facie Case for temporary injunction but erred in law in refusing the prayer for injunction on the wrong view of the matter, firstly, that if the plaintiff sustains any loss by use of offending mark by the defendants in the manufacture and sale of rickshaw tyres that could be compensated by way of damages and secondly, that the balance of convenience is also in favour of the defendants in that if injunction is granted as prayed for and the plaintiff ultimately fails to succeed in the suit he would not suffer anything whereas the defendants would be ruined. Mr Bhuiya submits that no amount of investment of money will entitle the defendants in law to infringe the Trade Mark of the plaintiff. He also submits with reference to various papers filed that the device being used by the defendants nearly resembles the registered Trade Mark within the mischief of section 21 of the Trade Mark Act, 1940, briefly the Act. In support of-his submission he cites the decisions in the case of Abdul Jobbar and another vs Ahmad Jail, PLD 1973 Karachi 289 and that of Messers Burney's Industrial and Commercial Co Ltd vs Messers Rehman Match Works, PLD 1983 Karachi 357: 

 7. Mr Azmalul Hossain, learned Senior Counsel for the respondents, on the other hand, submits in support of the impugned judgment and order refusing temporary injunction. He submits that the finding of the trial Court that the plaintiff has a prime facie case is wholly erroneous. By filing various papers, he submits that the device that is being used by the defendants in the manufacture and sale of the tyres is wholly distinct and dissimilar to that of the registered Trade Mark of the plaintiff in respect of name, picture features and design and get up and there is no scope for any confusion for deception. The plaintiff has failed to make out any case of infringement under section 21 of the Act. He also submits that on 29-10-2000 the defendants published their Trade Mark in the Daily 'Ittefaq' but the plaintiff did neither raise any objection nor inform them about any similarity of the Trade Marks and, as such, the plaintiff must be held to have consented to the use of their Trade Mark by implication under section 22(a) of the Act. He also submits that as per starch report supplied by the office of the Registrar dated 14-09-2000, it appears that other companies are also producing tyres using the device of single or double elephants but the plaintiff did not take any steps whatsoever against any of them. He also informs that on 20-09-2000 the defendants applied for registration of copyright of their tyres and on 20-12-2000 duly got registration with the device of double elephants facing each other with their trunks held high. They also got registration of Patent and Design. When the application of the defendants for registration is pending for disposal before the Registrar, the plaintiff could raise statutory objection before the Registrar under section 15 of the Act instead the institution of the suit is misconceived. Finally, he submits on the balance of convenience that various banks both national and international financed the enterprise of the defendants to the extent of 12 crore and if the manufacture and sale of their products remain suspended, the repayment schedule of the creditor banks would be affected and the existence of the industry would be endangered. He also cites the case of Dacca Match Factory vs Bangladesh Match Factory, 30 DLR 244 and that of De Cordova and others vs Vick Chemical Coy, Vol LXVIII No. 6 Reports of Patent, Design and Trade Mark Cases at page 103. 

 8. Learned Counsels argued on all probable issues that may be raised in the trial of the suit. It is neither necessary nor desirable to decide all questions raised. In an application under Order XXXIX rules 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure made on the allegations of infringement of Trade Marks, the Court is required to see whether the plaintiff is likely to succeed in the suit for Perpetual Injunction or not on prima facie proof of infringement of his registered Trade Mark within the mischief of section 21 of the Trade Marks Act, 1940 apart from the balance of convenience. It must also be noted that the concept of 'prima facie' case, as we generally understand by the phrase in civil proceedings, is no more relevant in Trade Marks cases. 

 9. In American Cyanamid Co vs Ethicon Lid 1975(1) All ER 504 (HL), the rule was formulated, it was sufficient if a "triable issue be presented by the plaintiff and the merits need not be gone into." 

 10. In UK Laddie, J reconsidered the principle recently and explained American Cyanamid in his judgment in Series 5 Software vs Clark, 1996(1) All ER 853 (Ch D). The learned Judge observed that in American Cyanamid, Lord Diplock did not lay down that the relative strength of the case of each party need not be gone into. In India, the Supreme Court of India in Colgate Palmolive (India) Ltd vs Hindustan Lever Ltd 1999(7) SCC 1 referred to Laddie, J's view and stated that the view of Laddie, J is correct and that American Cyanamid cannot be understood as having laid down anything inconsistent with the 'old practice'. Now, the Courts in England go into the question whether the plaintiff is likely or unlikely to win in the suit i.e. into the comparative strength of the case of the rival parties, apart from the question of balance of convenience. Therefore, in trade mark matters, it is now necessary to go into the question of 'comparable strength' of the cases of either party, apart from balance of convenience. 

 11. Comparative strength must be looked into on the basis of claims of the plaintiff made in the  application for injunction whether the use of the offending mark by the defendant is likely to infringe the Trade Mark rights of the plaintiff. 

 12. In the case before us, the learned Additional District Judge kept his decision pending for the suit on whether the defendant has caused infringement by use of 'Double Elephants' in the manufacture and sale of the rickshaw tyres within the meaning of section 21 of the Act. As the plaintiff has been manufacturing the tyres as proprietor of registered Trade Mark of Elephant since long and the application of the defendant for registration is still pending, so he found that the plaintiff has got a prima facie case for injunction. This finding was no doubt arrived at by the learned Additional District Judge on misconception of the principles applicable, as stated above, in such cases of Trade Mark, particularly, in the absence of any finding of infringement of the Trade Mark of the plaintiff. 

 13. Mr Ajmalul submits that the defendants gave an advertisement in the media and the plaintiff did not raise any objection thereto before the Registrar of Trade Marks. Had he raised any objection, he could have got his grievance redressed by the Registrar. In the absence of any such objection, the use of 'Double Elephants' by the defendant must be taken to be accepted by the plaintiff by implication under clause (a) of section 22 of the Act. Moreover, he submits that the suit of the plaintiff in view of section 15 of the Act must be held to be misconceived. Mr Bhuiyan submits in reply that seeing the advertisement, the suit was filed and injunction was prayed for. Remedies under section 15 of the Act cannot be supposed either to be alternative nor are the provisions of section 73 of the Act made subject to the section. 

 15. Both the learned Counsels have also addressed on the balance of convenience as stated earlier. Any decision on this issue is also dependent upon the main issue of infringement. It is also to be noted that if the offending Trade Mark of the defendants infringes the Trade Mark rights of the plaintiff within the meaning of section 21 of the Act, then no amount of monetary consideration can come in the way to restrain the defendants from using a Trade Mark even nearly resembling to that of the plaintiff. 

 16. On the infringement, both the learned Counsels submitted at length by submitting various papers and documents in support of their respective cases. Now the question is, whether the plaintiff could have been successful in making out a case of infringement of his registered Trade Mark as a proprietor against the defendant within the meaning of section 21 of the Act for temporary injunction. Mr Bhuiya submits that the plaintiff is proprietor of the Trade Mark of Elephant, single or double in the manufacture and sale of rickshaw tyres and the defendant has infringed his rights by use of such Elephant in manufacture and sale of the tyres. On the other hand, Mr Azmal submits that the defendant is producing and selling his rickshaw tyres using the marks of 'Double Elephants' and this mark is so distinct and dissimilar to that of the plaintiff that there is no chance of any confusion in the minds of the consumers about whose tyres they are buying for they buy by the name i.e. GAZI or HAMZA tyres. 

 17. As stated earlier, learned Additional District Judge has not given any decision on the moot issue of infringement, i.e. whether the Trade Mark being used by the defendants at least nearly resembles to the registered Trade Mark of the plaintiff or not or whether the plaintiff has got any chance to succeed in the suit or not. Now, the question facing me, whether I should decide, of course, for the purpose of this appeal, such issue when the suit is nearly ready for hearing. I have given my anxious consideration to the matter. I could not be sure any decision of mine on such issues would not affect the decisions in the trial of the suit. At last, I have come to this opinion that if I can dispose of the appeal without deciding the issue, I should follow that path. 

 18. Mr Bhuiyan submits that the defendants have been producing and selling their tyres for long, and having come to know that the plaintiff instituted the suit. He also submits showing the latest search report dated 09-06-2001 obtained from the office of the Registrar that six companies are producing and selling rickshaw tyres using Trade Mark of Elephant, double or single and of them, the Trade Mark of the plaintiff only is registered and applications of others including that of the defendant for registration is pending. Mr Azmal submits that the suit is now posted for SD on 03-07-2001 next, which is not denied by Mr Bhuiyan. If the parties are now left free of any opinion of this Division to fight out their cases within few months on the issue of infringement before the Additional District Judge, none of them appears to be prejudiced. In such circumstances, the impugned order of learned District Judge refusing temporary injunction does not call for any interference. This appeal therefore fails.
